module_title: Advanced Analysis - Plate Tectonics, Syntaxial Bends, and Purvanchal
introduction: This advanced level focuses on the geological mechanics of the Himalayan formation, the structural fault lines separating the ranges, and the eastward extension known as the Purvanchal Hills.

core_concepts.title: Plate Tectonics & The Tethys Sea
core_concepts.description: The Himalayas were formed by the collision of the northward-drifting 'Indo-Australian Plate' with the massive 'Eurasian Plate'. The marine sediments accumulated in the 'Tethys Sea' (which lay between them) were compressed and uplifted to form these fold mountains.

core_concepts.title: Syntaxial Bends (Hairpin Bends)
core_concepts.description: The Himalayas do not fade out gradually. At their western and eastern extremities, they take sudden, sharp southward bends. The western bend is near Nanga Parbat (Indus gorge), and the eastern bend is near Namcha Barwa (Brahmaputra gorge).

core_concepts.title: The Purvanchal (Eastern Hills)
core_concepts.description: Beyond the Dihang gorge, the Himalayas bend sharply to the south and spread along the eastern boundary of India. Composed mostly of strong sandstones, they comprise the Patkai Bum, Naga Hills, Manipur Hills, and Mizo Hills.

core_concepts.title: Structural Fault Lines
core_concepts.description: The Himalayan ranges are separated by deep fault lines. The Main Central Thrust (MCT) separates the Great and Lesser Himalayas. The Main Boundary Fault (MBF) separates the Lesser Himalayas and Shiwaliks. The Himalayan Frontal Fault (HFF) separates the Shiwaliks from the Northern Plains.

important_entities.name: Marine Fossils in the Himalayas
important_entities.significance: The presence of marine fossils (like ammonites) at altitudes of 8,000 meters proves that the rock layers of the Himalayas were once at the bottom of the ancient Tethys Sea.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A classic UPSC trap. The Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya are structurally NOT a part of the Himalayas or Purvanchal. They are an eastward extension of the ancient Peninsular Plateau.

The Himalayas are not structurally dead. The Indo-Australian plate is still pushing into the Eurasian plate. Therefore, the Himalayas are still rising by a few centimeters every year, making the region highly vulnerable to earthquakes (Seismic Zone V).

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Many Cats Think (MCT), Many Bears Fall (MBF), Horses Fly Fast (HFF)

exam_strategy_tips: In Assertion-Reasoning questions, link the 'frequent earthquakes in the Himalayan region' directly to the 'ongoing convergence of tectonic plates'.
Remember the exact locations of the Syntaxial Bends: Nanga Parbat in the West and Namcha Barwa in the East.
